title: Hearts at rest
hookLine: in the remembrance of Allah hearts find rest (13:28)

lines: A GLASS THAT KEEPS GETTING BUMPED.
cards: It's late. The house is quiet, the phone is face down, and your mind is doing laps. The email you didn't answer.
The thing someone said at lunch. The bill. Back to the email.
Nothing is broken. The heart just won't settle, like a glass of water on a table that keeps getting bumped. Surah ar-Ra'd has a verse for that hour.
It's short, and it doesn't promise the email goes away.

teach.b: Verse twenty-eight, in Pickthall's translation: "Who have believed and whose hearts have rest in the remembrance of Allah. Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!"

The key word is tatma'innu, find rest, from itmi'nan, a settled calm, the stillness of something that has stopped shaking. It's the same root as the soul at rest at the end of Surah al-Fajr, which you met last year.
It appears in al-Baqarah too, when Ibrahim asks God to show him how He gives life to the dead. God asks: do you not believe?

teach.h: IBRAHIM: THAT MY HEART MAY REST.
teach.b: Ibrahim says: yes, but so that my heart may be at rest. Even a prophet wanted that settling.

The means is dhikr, remembrance: calling God to mind in the prayer, in reading the Qur'an, and in short phrases repeated through the day. Subhanallah, glory be to God. Alhamdulillah, praise belongs to God.
La ilaha illallah, no god but God. Notice the shape of the verse.
It says the remembrance of Allah twice, and in the second half the Arabic puts those words before the verb: it is in God's remembrance that hearts find rest.
Some commentators read that order as emphasis: there, and not elsewhere. Another verse adds a promise that runs both ways: remember Me, and I will remember you.
And a hadith in Bukhari puts it starkly: the one who remembers his Lord and the one who doesn't are like the living and the dead. The verse doesn't say the world calms down. It says the heart can.
The glass can stop shaking, even while the table is still being bumped.

how: Muslims practice dhikr after the daily prayers and through the day, repeating phrases such as subhanallah, alhamdulillah and la ilaha illallah, often counting on the fingers or on prayer beads; Sufi orders also gather for dhikr together.

o: a deep sleep that comes after long prayer
a settled calm, like water that has stopped shaking
a life with no problems left to worry about

games.q: hearts at rest — tap the pairs.
p: asked so his heart might be at rest

s: 13:28 promises the world will calm down
it says hearts find rest in God's remembrance, not that the troubles stop.
a prophet in the Qur'an asks for his heart to be at rest
Ibrahim: yes, I believe, but so that my heart may be at rest (2:260).
the remembrance of God is mentioned twice in 13:28
and the second time it comes first, for emphasis: there, hearts find rest.

games.q: God asks Ibrahim: do you not believe? Ibrahim has just asked to see how the dead are raised. what does he answer?
o: yes, but so that my heart may be at rest.
I only want proof for my people.
games.why: yes, but so that my heart may be at rest. the same word as 13:28: itmi'nan, a settled calm.

practice: If you pray, repeat one short phrase quietly with the breath, subhanallah, alhamdulillah or la ilaha illallah, counting on your fingers if that helps. If you'd rather not, choose one word that brings you to stillness.
When the mind wanders off to the email, come back; coming back is the practice.

wordCard.voice: Itmi'nan. The settled calm hearts find in remembering God, 13:28's promise, the stillness of something that has stopped shaking. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "hearts find rest" (13:28), from itmi'nan, a settled calm.

carryVoice: Your line: hearts rest in remembering. Even a prophet asked for that. Day four hundred forty-four, done.
